scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El «Año Cero»: hacia el verano de 1977 el punk ya era una parodia de sí mismo y su frágil alianza entre chicos obreros y bohemios de escuela de arte se rompe. De un lado quedan los «punks verdaderos», populistas, que desembocarán en el Oi! y el hardcore; del otro, la vanguardia que se llamará postpunk, que vio en 1977 no un retorno al rock crudo sino la ocasión de romper con la tradición. Su legado común: la fe en el poder de la música y el «hazlo tú mismo».

podcast.title: Birth and Early Life – May 10, 1957, London
podcast.body: Simon John Richie was born in London on May 10, 1957. His father, John Richie, was a soldier in the Royal Guard, and his mother, Anne McDonald (later Anne Beverly), was a free-spirited hippie who had worked for the Royal Air Force. He was born without his parents ever being married. "Simon John Richie was born in London on May 10, 1957."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mother's Heroin Addiction – By Spring 1962
podcast.body: After returning to the UK, Sid's mother Anne scammed the National Health Service by pretending to be a junkie to get free housing. She then fully embraced the role and became a heroin addict by the spring of 1962, when Sid was about five years old. "Anne ended up being a heroin addict by the spring of 1962."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stepfather's Death – 1965
podcast.body: In late 1964, his mother Anne married Christopher Beverly, which explained why his mother was known as Anne Beverly while Sid's birth name remained Richie. Christopher Beverly died of cancer about six months after the wedding, a few weeks before paperwork could be filed for him to adopt Sid. "Christopher Richie died of cancer about six months after the wedding and a few weeks before the paperwork would be filed so he could adopt Sid."

podcast.title: Drummer for Siouxsie and the Banshees Debut – September 1976
podcast.body: Sid played drums for Siouxsie and the Banshees at their debut performance in September 1976. This was one of his early musical involvements before joining the Sex Pistols. "He was the drummer for Susie in the Banshees when they made their debut in September of 1976."

podcast.title: Joining Sex Pistols as Bassist – February 1977
podcast.body: After Glenn Matlock was fired from the Sex Pistols in February 1977, manager Malcolm McLaren decided to replace him with a fan. Sid was chosen because he was always around and was Johnny Rotten's friend, embodying the punk ethos of the ultimate fan joining the ultimate band. "Malcolm McLaren came up with the idea of hiring one of the group's fans as his replacement."

podcast.title: Arrested for Second-Degree Murder – October 13, 1978
podcast.body: Sid Vicious was charged with second-degree murder for Nancy Spungen's death on October 13, 1978, and sent to the detox unit at Rikers Island Prison. Bail was set at $50,000. "Sid was charged with second-degree murder and sent to the detox unit at Rikers Island Prison."

podcast.title: Assault on Patti Smith's Brother – December 9, 1978
podcast.body: On December 9, 1978, Sid got into a fight with the brother of singer Patti Smith during a night out and slashed his face with a beer bottle. He was arrested on felony assault charges and sent back to Rikers Island. "They get into a fight and Sid slashes the guy's face with a beer bottle."

podcast.title: Disappearance and Overdose After Breakup – January 1978
podcast.body: Hours after the Sex Pistols broke up on January 14, 1978, Sid disappeared until he was found comatose in a closet in the Haight-Ashbury district. While attempting to fly back to London, he managed to overdose on the plane during a connection in New York. "He disappeared until someone found him comatose in a closet somewhere in the high-dashberry district."

podcast.title: Drug-Induced Incidents on American Tour (1978)
podcast.body: During the Sex Pistols' ill-fated American tour, Sid Vicious frequently became so heavily intoxicated that he was physically assaulted by his own bodyguard. These incidents underscored the chaotic and dysfunctional nature of the tour, contributing to the overall animosity within the band. "Sid Vicious kept getting so wasted that he managed to get beat up by his own bodyguard."

podcast.title: Involvement in Nancy Spungen's Death (October 12, 1978)
podcast.body: Sid Vicious, bassist for the Sex Pistols, was implicated in the death of his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, who was found stabbed to death in room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on October 12, 1978. Sid and Nancy were both heroin and Tuinal addicts, and on the night of her death, Sid reportedly took up to 52 Tuinal tablets, which would have rendered him unconscious. Although he initially confessed, his level of incapacitation made it unlikely he remembered. He was arrested and charged with Nancy's murder but died of a heroin overdose before the trial could commence. "Sid was arrested, charged with Nancy's murder, and then died of a heroin overdose before things could go to trial."

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren Posts Bail – October 17, 1978
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren posted Sid's $50,000 bail, leading to his release from Rikers Island on October 17, 1978. "October 17, 1978. Malcolm McLaren posts Sid's bail and he's released."

podcast.title: Move to New York City – August 1978
podcast.body: With nowhere to go after their eviction, Sid and Nancy decided to move to New York City in August 1978, a place where Nancy claimed to know people. This move was partly funded by a £10,000 loan from Malcolm McLaren. "With nowhere to go, they decided that it was time to move to New York."

podcast.title: Death by Heroin Overdose (February 2, 1979)
podcast.body: Sid Vicious died at 21 years old from a heroin overdose. He was out on bail awaiting trial for the murder of his girlfriend Nancy Spungen. After 55 days in Riker's Island prison, a completely detoxed Sid was released on February 1, 1979, and celebrated his freedom with his mom Beverly, new girlfriend Michelle Robinson, and friends at Michelle's apartment at 63 Bank Street in New York. His mom called over English photographer and dealer Peter Codic to deliver heroin for him. Sid took a "taste" as a dessert, but due to his detoxed state, his body was super vulnerable to the 99% pure heroin, causing him to overdose. They revived him and put him to bed, which was a fatal move as he should have been kept awake until the drug left his system. The next morning, February 2, he was found stone-cold dead in bed next to Michelle. "Apparently the heroin he took the night before was 99% pure. And since he had detoxed, his body was super vulnerable."

podcast.body: On the morning of February 2nd, 1979, his mother discovered Sid Vicious stone-cold dead in bed next to Michelle Robinson. As he slept, his heart beat slower and slower, and his lungs filled up with fluid, leading to his death. "February 2nd, 1979, Groundhog Day, Sid's mum comes into check on her boy and he's lying in bed next to Michelle. And he was stone-cold dead."

podcast.body: A suicide note was reportedly found in the pocket of Sid Vicious's leather jacket after his death, referring to Nancy Spungen and a "death pact." The note expressed his intention to keep his half of the bargain and requested to be buried next to Nancy, in his leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. "It read, We had a death pact referring to Nancy. I have to keep my half of the bargain. Please bury me next to my baby. Burry me in my leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. Goodbye."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: American Tour Disaster – Uncontrollable Behavior
podcast.body: Sid was completely uncontrollable during the Sex Pistols' ill-fated 12-day American tour through the conservative South. He got into an altercation with Georgia police, was repeatedly beaten by his own bodyguards after baiting them, and his major heroin dependency, exacerbated by Nancy Spungen, made him miserable and strung out. "Sid was uncontrollable for the entire 12 days the van was on the road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrest and Imprisonment for Nancy Spungen Murder
podcast.body: Sid Vicious, at 21 years old, was arrested and charged with the murder of his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, and spent about seven weeks in the detox section of Reikers Island Prison. Spungen's body was discovered in the bathroom of room 100 at the Chelsea Hotel on October 12, 1978, having bled out after being stabbed in the abdomen with Sid's knife. Both were heavily intoxicated that night, and Sid claimed no memory of the event, leading to various theories including his alleged confession, involvement of a drug dealer, suicide attempt, or a robbery from which a chunk of cash was missing. "Her body was found in the bathroom of room 100 at the Chelsea Hotel on the morning of October 12, 1978. She'd blight out after being stabbed in the abdomen with a knife owned by Sid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Art School and Meeting Future Punks – Before Dropping Out
podcast.body: Before dropping out of art school, Sid met John Liden (later Johnny Rotten) and John Wardle (later Jah Wobble) in his classes. He also hung out with a fourth John, John Gray, who later lived a more traditional life. "Before he dropped out of art school, John met another couple of John's in some of his classes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Aspiring Male Model – Despite Appearance
podcast.body: Despite having bad skin and awful acne, Sid seriously wanted to become a male model. He would wear sandals in winter to show off his weird nail polish and dyed his hair red like David Bowie. "He wanted to be a model. Seriously, he wanted to be a male model."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Assault on Nick Kent
podcast.body: In June 1976, Sid Vicious assaulted music journalist Nick Kent of the NME with a rusted bicycle chain after disliking his trousers. Despite the severity of the attack, Sid escaped charges. "said when up to him and said, boy, I don't like your trousers. And bashed him up pretty good with the rusted bicycle chain that he carried with him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Assault on Todd Smith's Girlfriend
podcast.body: On December 5, 1978, while supervised by Rockets Red Glare at a club, Sid Vicious got into a fight using a beer bottle with the girlfriend of Todd Smith, the brother of singer Patti Smith. He was arrested, charged with assault, and sent to Riker's Island. "On December 5th, he went to a club under the supervision of Rockets Red Glare and got into a beer bottle fight with the girlfriend of Todd Smith, the brother of singer Patty Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Attack on NME Journalist Nick Kent – Over Clothing
podcast.body: Sid once physically attacked Nick Kent, a journalist with the NME, with his motorcycle chain simply because he disliked Kent's pants. "In other case, he took his motorcycle chain to Nick Kent, a journalist with the NME because he didn't like his pants."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Banned from American Airlines and Holiday Inn – Due to Self-Destruction
podcast.body: By the time the Sex Pistols reached San Francisco on their American tour, the band had been banned from both American Airlines and the entire Holiday Inn chain, largely because Sid had redefined self-destructive behavior. "The group had been banned from American Airlines and the entire holiday in chain. Partly because Sid had rewritten the book on self-destruction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bass Strings Broken on Stage – Dallas Gig
podcast.body: During a Sex Pistols gig at the Longhorn Ballroom in Dallas on January 10, 1978, three of the four strings on Sid's bass were broken. He either didn't notice or didn't care, or it was irrelevant because a roadie was playing his parts backstage. "At one point during the gig, three of the four strings on Sid's bass were broken."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Beaten by Bodyguard (While on tour)
podcast.body: Sid Vicious was described as such a difficult person that he was once beaten up by his own bodyguard while on tour. "he was such a jerk that he managed to get beaten up by his own bodyguard when he was on tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brutal Beating from Bodyguard
podcast.body: Sid Vicious challenged his bodyguard, Glenn Allison, a large Vietnam vet, to a fight. Allison responded by severely beating Sid, grabbing him by the throat, smashing his head against the ceiling, and then against a sink multiple times, after which Sid, bleeding, expressed admiration for Allison and sought friendship. "Allison began by grabbing Sid by the throat and smacked his head up against the ceiling. And when Allison finished pummeling Sid's head against a sink half a dozen times, Sid said through bloody teeth, you're good enough. I like you. Now we can be friends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Charged with Murder - Died Awaiting Trial
podcast.body: Despite his claims, Sid was charged with Nancy's murder. However, he died of an overdose on February 2, 1979, while still awaiting trial, leading the New York police to consider the case closed. "Still Sid was charged with her murder, but he died of an overdose on February 2nd, 1979 while still awaiting trial. The New York cops have always been satisfied that Sid was the murderer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Charged with Nancy Spungen's Murder
podcast.body: In October 1978, after Nancy Spungen's death (either by suicide or murder), Sid Vicious was charged with her murder and incarcerated at Rikers Island Prison in New York, which temporarily provided him with food and accommodation. "When Nancy either committed suicide or was killed in October of 1978, Sid was charged with her murder and sent to Riker's Island Prison in New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Childhood in Ibiza and UK – Early 1960s
podcast.body: Sid, his mother Anne, and his biological father John Richie planned to move to Ibiza. Anne and Sid went ahead, but John Richie never joined them. In Ibiza, Anne worked as a typist and sold pre-rolled joints to tourists, eventually getting deported back to the UK due to lack of money to settle. "The three of them moved to the Spanish island of Ibiza, or at least that was the plan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death Anniversary Mentioned
podcast.body: Anniversaries of the death of Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols were among the milestones discussed. "anniversaries of the deaths of people like Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols and Ian Curtis of Joy Division"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death at 21 Years Old – Before Murder Trial
podcast.body: Sid Vicious died at the age of 21 on February 2, 1979, from a heroin overdose. His death occurred before he could stand trial for the murder of Nancy Spungen, leading the New York police to close the case. "Sid was dead before he got to go to trial for the murder of Nancy Spungin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death by Heroin Overdose
podcast.body: Died in his sleep around 3 AM on February 2, 1979, at 63 Bank Street in Greenwich Village, New York. His death was caused by an overdose of "ultra pure heroin," which was reportedly provided by his mother, on the night before his murder trial was scheduled to begin. "At some point during the night, he overdosed in some ultra pure heroin that his mom had so thoughtfully provided and died in his sleep sometime around three the next morning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Deeper Drug Stupor – Marijuana, Methadone, Heroin, Dilaudid
podcast.body: As Sid's musical endeavors stalled due to Nancy's interference, both of them sank deeper into a stupor of multiple drugs, including marijuana, methadone, heroin, and Dilaudid. "Both of them sank deeper into a stupor of marijuana, methadone, heroin, and delauded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Denial and Alibi - Overdose
podcast.body: Sid claimed to have no knowledge of the murder, stating he had taken 20 pills earlier that morning and passed out completely around 3 AM, remaining unconscious until 9:30 AM, while a party supposedly continued in the room with people coming and going all night. "Now Sid claimed to know nothing about this. He had taken 20 pills earlier in the morning and it passed out completely, even though there was something of a party going on in the room and there were people coming in going all night. Sid passed out at around 3 and he didn't get off that bed until 9.30 in the morning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Doubts About Nancy's Murder – Alternate Theories
podcast.body: Despite being charged, doubts persist about whether Sid actually murdered Nancy. Theories include Nancy plunging the knife into herself while high, or a drug dealer named Rockets Redgler (or Michael) being responsible, as suggested by the 2004 book "Too Fast to Live" and the film "Who Killed Nancy." "I think it's one of those things where, you know, when you're nodded out and you're, you know, on smack that... She could have as easily plunged it into herself and not even felt it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Use and Peculiar Diet on Tour
podcast.body: During the Sex Pistols' American tour, Sid Vicious was deeply involved in drug use, developed a taste for groupies, and would typically eat three knickerbocker glories (an ice cream dessert) at a time, mounted on the table. "I'll never forget the day in America. I think it was somewhere near San Antonio on the last ill-fated tour they had that Sid at that time got involved in the world of drugs, naturally inclined to develop a taste for groupies and ultimately met a peril. But that time was very out to lunch and would only eat nica-bocker glories and usually three in one go and they would be mounted on the table."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Life & Family Background
podcast.body: Born John Simon Richie on May 10, 1957. His mother, Ann, was a high school dropout who became a pot dealer and later a hardcore heroin addict. His father, John, a guardsman at Buckingham Palace and semi-pro trombone player, never supported them after Sid's birth in Ibiza, Spain. "His mother Ann was a high school dropout who met Sid's father while she was enlisted in the army. His father, John, was, believe it or not, a guardsman at Buckingham Palace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Early Musical Ventures
podcast.body: Before joining the Sex Pistols, Sid and John Lighten (Johnny Rotten) busked, often playing Alice Cooper covers on acoustic guitar and tambourine. Their method was to play until they were paid to stop. "Sid and John Lighten picked up some spare change busking, usually by playing covers by Alice Cooper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Enforced Detoxification
podcast.body: After being released on bail in November 1978, Sid Vicious assaulted someone with a smashed beer bottle, leading to his re-arrest and a period of enforced detoxification at Reikers Island Prison, which he completed before his final release. "he was sent to Reikers for a period of enforced detoxification. After completing that rehab, he was released on that Thursday, February 1st."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evicted by Jah Wobble – With an Axe
podcast.body: After the Paris trip, Sid and Nancy were evicted from a flat they were sharing with others by Sid's old friend, Jah Wobble. Wobble, fed up with Nancy especially, chased them out of the apartment with an axe. "So he chased the two of them out of the apartment with an axe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Failed Marriage to Chrissie Hynde
podcast.body: Sid was paid two pounds by Chrissie Hynde, who was working illegally in the UK, to marry her for a work permit. The marriage almost happened, but the office was closed on the day they intended to go through with it. "She paid Sid two pounds to marry her so she could get a work permit. And it almost happened too, but the day they went to get married, the office was closed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Fashion Victimness – David Bowie and Roxy Music Influence
podcast.body: Sid was initially very focused on fashion, particularly styles inspired by David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust and Aladdin Sane periods. He was also a huge fan of Roxy Music and would steal Vogue magazines, often getting fashion details wrong. "He was really into clothes, especially the styles inspired by David Bowie through his Ziggy Stardust in the Latin St period."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Filming for "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle" – Paris Trip
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren had the idea for Sid to continue as the new singer for the Sex Pistols. Sid traveled to Paris to film sequences for the movie "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle," performing Eddie Cochran songs. This trip was awful due to Sid and Malcolm's animosity and Nancy's continued drug supply. "The Sex Pistols could carry on with Sid as the new singer. So it was off to Paris in a cloud of junk to film a couple of sequences for a film that would end up being called the Great Rock and Roll Swindle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Overdose and Suicide Note
podcast.body: On February 2, 1979, after a celebratory party at Michelle Robinson's apartment following his detox program and release from Riker's Island, Sid Vicious overdosed on heroin. He left a suicide note stating, "bury me in my leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. Goodbye." He was 21 years old. "Sid left a note that read, bury me in my leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. Goodbye."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Glass-Throwing Incident at 100 Club
podcast.body: On the second day of the 100 Club Punk Special in September 1976, while The Damned were performing, a speed-intoxicated Sid Vicious threw a glass aimed at Dave Vanian, the singer. He missed Vanian but hit a woman in the face, blinding her in one eye, which led to Sid's first prison sentence. "He missed hitting a woman in the face and blinding her in one eye. That led to Sid's first taste of prison."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Growing Post-Mortem Legend and Merchandising
podcast.body: Following his death, Sid Vicious's legend grew "to enormous proportions," resulting in numerous books and movies about him, and his face being featured on "a million t-shirts." "This then, Sid's legend has grown to enormous proportions. Books have been written about him. Movies have been made about him. His face has been on a million t-shirts..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Heroin Addiction
podcast.body: Sid Vicious developed a severe heroin addiction while he was with the Sex Pistols. After the band broke up, his addiction continued, impacting his ability to maintain a responsible or coherent life with his American girlfriend, Nancy Spungen.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Hospitalization for Overdose – New York
podcast.body: Sid overdosed at least once in New York and was subsequently sent to the hospital. "Sid OD, at least once that month, and was sent to hospital."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Incident at a Texas Truck Stop – Slashed a Man's Arm
podcast.body: During the American tour near San Antonio, Sid, strung out and high, slashed a man's arm with a pen knife at a truck stop restaurant because the man and his family made rude comments about Sid's appearance. Blood sprayed "like ketchup" over the man's steak, nearly inciting a riot among long-distance truck drivers. "He went round to the back of the gentleman that was eating his steak and chips and pulled his sleeve back and threw his arm over and above the man's head and over the man's plate up fairly high and withdrew a pen knife from his pocket and slashed his arm and all the blood blew out like ketchup over the man's steak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Infamous Murder - Nancy Spungen
podcast.body: Sid Vicious is central to one of the most infamous murders in music history, involving his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen. "This is probably the most infamous murder in all of music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Infamous Truck Stop Encounter
podcast.body: During the ill-fated US tour, Sid Vicious, heavily involved in drugs, engaged in shocking behavior at a truck stop restaurant near San Antonio. After a family complained about his smell and made rude comments, Sid approached the father, slashed his arm with a penknife, causing blood to splatter over the man's steak. "And all the blood blew out like ketchup over the man's steak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Intellectual Interests – Reading and Space Race
podcast.body: Despite his later reputation, Sid was not unintelligent. He enjoyed reading books by Edgar Allan Poe and followed the American Space Race with significant interest. "He loved reading books by Edgar Allan Poe and watched the American Space Race with great interest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Interview with Johnny Rotten – Before Final San Francisco Show
podcast.body: Before the final Sex Pistols show in San Francisco, Sid was coherent enough to do an interview with Johnny Rotten at a local radio station. However, the interview became ugly and aggressive. "Sid was straight enough to do an interview with Johnny at a local radio station. But it got ugly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Life in Hackney, London – Late 1960s
podcast.body: Around five years after Christopher Beverly's death, Sid and his mother moved to Hackney in the East End of London, where they lived without many luxuries. His mother made extra money by rolling joints for dealers she knew and continued her occasional heroin use. "Mom made some extra dodge by rolling joints for the dealers that she knew."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Life of Poverty and Petty Crime
podcast.body: During his final months and for most of his life, Sid Vicious lived in "almost total poverty." He was characterized as a junkie, a petty thief, and a violent individual who "really didn't have much use for manners." "The most infamous dead punk of all time was basically living hand to mouth during the last months of his life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Limited Income After Sex Pistols
podcast.body: After the Sex Pistols disbanded in January 1978, Sid Vicious lacked a reliable income source. He did not contribute to writing any of the band's songs, meaning he received no significant royalty checks. Furthermore, the financial arrangements made by the band's manager, Malcolm McLaren, provided him with very little income. He relied on the generosity of friends and meager earnings from solo performances, with any money going towards rent, food, music gear, and heroin. "He was reduced to relying on the kindness of friends and to the meager amounts he received as a solo performer in the post sex pistols world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Limited Musical Ability – Tambourine and Acoustic Guitar
podcast.body: Before joining the Sex Pistols, Sid was not much into playing music. When busking with the other Johns, he could only play the tambourine. When given an acoustic guitar, he could not play it. "Sid really couldn't do anything but play the tambourine, although they did once give him an acoustic guitar, which he could not play."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Meeting Nancy's Parents – Philadelphia
podcast.body: Sid and Nancy traveled to Philadelphia for Sid to meet Nancy's parents. The meeting was strained, and after a few hours, it was suggested the couple stay at a Holiday Inn instead of the family guest room. "They also went to Philadelphia, so Sid could meet the parents. That must have been interesting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Member of Flowers of Romance – Early Band
podcast.body: Sid was also part of a group called Flowers of Romance, another one of his early band projects in the burgeoning punk scene. "And he was also part of a group called Flowers of Romance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Missed Audition for The Damned – Lead Singer Opportunity
podcast.body: Sid was considered for the role of lead singer in the new punk band The Damned but failed to show up for the audition and did not get the gig. "It's also possible that he was considered to be the lead singer of another new punk band called The Damned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mother Smuggles Drugs to Rikers Island – In Her Boots
podcast.body: While Sid was imprisoned at Rikers Island, his mother Anne was a regular visitor. She smuggled dope into the prison inside her boots, which Sid would conceal and then use to get high in his cell. "She smuggled in dope in her boots. Sid took the drugs and stuck them, well you know where, and then he went back to his cell and got high."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Moved to Room 100, Chelsea Hotel – After Mattress Fire
podcast.body: By October 11, 1978, Sid and Nancy had moved into room 100 at the Chelsea Hotel because the mattress in their previous room had caught fire. "By October 11th, 1978, Sid and Nancy had moved into room 100 at the Chelsea Hotel. See the mattress in their old room caught fire, wonder how that happened, and they had to move."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Confusion – Simon John Richie vs. John Simon Richie
podcast.body: While widely known as John Simon Richie, his birth certificate actually states Simon John Richie. The mix-up of his names remains a mystery, and he also referred to himself as John Richie, John Beverly, or "Simon Something" at different times. "I know a lot of people say John Simon Richie, but it's Simon John Richie on his birth certificates."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nancy's Managerial Interference – Scaring Off Labels
podcast.body: Nancy Spungen acted as Sid's manager in New York but her outrageous demands and behavior alienated the press and scared away record companies. This made it impossible for Sid to form a lasting band. "As Sid's manager, she started throwing her weight around, depending on all sorts of outrageous things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New Band in New York – With New York Dolls and The Clash Members
podcast.body: Within a week of arriving in New York, Sid was serious about his music career and formed a new band. This group included two members from the New York Dolls and Mick Jones of The Clash. "Within a week, he had a band together, consisting of two guys from the New York Dolls and Mick Jones of the Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nickname Origin
podcast.body: John Beverly's nickname "Sid" came from an incident where he was bitten by John Lighten's pet hamster, also named Sid, which led to the observation, "Who knew that a hamster could be vicious?" The "Vicious" part was added later, inspired by a Lou Reed song. "From that day on, John Beverly had the nickname Sid. The vicious came later after the Lureed song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Ongoing Controversy and Alternative Theories
podcast.body: Many people dispute the official police conclusion, and private investigations have offered different conclusions, with drug dealer Rockets Red Glare (Michael Mora) being a primary alternative suspect. "There are however a lot of people who say that's crap. There have been a number of private investigations and a number of different conclusions have been reached, so if it wasn't Sid, who was it?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of "Sid Vicious" Name – From John Liden's Hamster
podcast.body: John Liden gave him the name Sid Vicious. The "Sid" part came from Liden's pet hamster, who bit Sid one day, prompting Sid to exclaim, "Oh, Sid is really vicious!" "The Sid parts came from John Liden's pet hamster who bit Sid one day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Perpetual Label as Murderer
podcast.body: Regardless of the unresolved doubts and alternative theories, Sid Vicious will forever be associated with the murder of his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, a truth that "we'll never, ever really know." "But we'll never, ever really know, will we? On that note, here's a statement from the punk rock band, The Exploited. This is called Sidvicious was innocent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Playing Bass with Sex Pistols – Doubts about Musicianship
podcast.body: Sid played bass for the Sex Pistols through most of 1977 and during tours in Britain and Scandinavia. However, he was notoriously inept, often drunk and high, leading to significant doubt whether he ever actually played notes on stage. For some shows, a roadie was hired to play his parts offstage and unseen. "Basically Sid was so inept as a musician, often so drunk and high that there's real doubt whether he ever played a note on stage with the pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pogo Dance Inventor – Public Proclamation
podcast.body: After joining the Sex Pistols, one of the first things Sid Vicious did was publicly declare himself the inventor of the Pogo, a punk dance characterized by jumping up and down in place. "One of the first things he did after joining the band was publicly proclaim himself as the inventor of the Pogo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Death Assistance
podcast.body: Jerry Only of the Miss Fitz, who owned the only car in New York at the time (his mother's old brown station wagon), drove Sid's mother to the coroner and later helped her visit the cemetery where Nancy Spungen was buried, where she spread some of Sid's ashes. "He was the only person in New York who had a car, his mum's old brown station wagon. So he drove Sid's mum to the coroner and later helped her visit the cemetery where Nancy was buried."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Pistols Coma and Hospitalization
podcast.body: On January 19, 1978, while flying to London after the Sex Pistols disbanded, Sid fell into a coma due to an overdose of diazepam, methadone, and alcohol. He was rushed to a hospital upon landing and warned that continued drinking would lead to his death within six months. "But on the flight, he fell into a coma. Too much dyes of Pam, methadone, and alcohol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Posthumous Financial Gain
podcast.body: Born May 10, 1957, and died February 2, 1979. Despite being unable to afford a McDonald's hamburger when he died, he now earns money as a "dead guy" through royalties from a couple of live solo CDs and "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle." "Sid could barely afford to buy a hamburger when he died. A hamburger had McDonald's. And now he's looking down. Or actually probably looking up. Wondering why he's now making all this money as a dead guy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Posthumous Icon Status
podcast.body: Sid Vicious died just over three months before his 22nd birthday. His death solidified his status as a punk icon, inspiring numerous books and movies about him and Nancy, and cementing his legend within the punk movement.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Punk's James Dean and Symbol of Self-Destruction – Legacy
podcast.body: Sid Vicious became an icon after his death, selling millions of t-shirts annually. He is remembered as "punk's answer to James Dean" for his "live fast, die young, die hard" mentality and as a symbol of the original punk movement's inherent drive towards self-destruction. "First of all, he was punk's answer to James Dean. Live fast, die young, die hard."

podcast.title: Real Name and Nickname Origin
podcast.body: Sid Vicious's birth name was John Simon Richie. His friend Johnny Lydon (Johnny Rotten) gave him the nickname "Sid" after Lydon's pet hamster. The "Vicious" part of his name was inspired by a Lou Reed song. Despite being initially "quite a gentle guy," Richie felt compelled to live up to the "Vicious" title.

xref.title: Murder at Chelsea Hotel (October 12, 1978)
xref.body: Nancy Spungen, girlfriend of Sid Vicious, was found dead from a single stab wound to her stomach in room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on October 12, 1978. Nancy had a troubled life, diagnosed with schizophrenia at 15 and supporting herself through prostitution from age 17 before becoming a groupie to bands like The Ramones, New York Dolls, and Aerosmith. She became inseparable from Sid Vicious for 19 months, and they both were heroin and Tuinal addicts. On the night of October 11, 1978, several people visited their room, and Sid allegedly took up to 52 Tuinal tablets, completely incapacitating him. At around 2:30 am on October 12th, Nancy asked Rockets Redglare, their drug connection and Sid's bodyguard, for Dilaudid. Later, around 7:30 am, female moans were heard, and at 10 am, Sid called the front desk. Nancy was found stabbed and bleeding to death, in a weird angle under the bathroom sink. Sid initially confessed but was likely too incapacitated. The theory later emerged that Rockets Redglare, who died in 2007, was the murderer, allegedly stabbing Nancy with Sid's Bowie knife during an argument over stolen cash, a confession he reportedly made while drinking at CBGB. "Nancy Spungin, girlfriend of ex-sex Bristol Sidvicious, at the Chelsea Hotel on October 12, 1978."

"She had been stabbed in the stomach by a big knife, a knife owned by Sid. It wasn't ugly wound. She must have taken hours to die."

xref.title: Sid Vicious Ashes Allegedly Spilled at Heathrow Terminal 4 (February 1979)
xref.body: After Sid Vicious's death on February 2, 1979 (heroin overdose while awaiting trial for the murder of Nancy Spungen), his mother Anne Beverly had him cremated. Two weeks later, allegedly drunk while returning to London through Heathrow Airport, she tripped, fell, and spilled Sid's ashes in the terminal — some reportedly embedded in the carpet and sucked into the ventilation system. Rumor holds that Sid Dust still circulates through Terminal 4. However, those with knowledge say this is not what happened: what is confirmed is that before returning to England, Anne took his ashes to Nancy Spungen's grave in Philadelphia and spread them there. What is also confirmed is that New York police tipped off London police, who raided Anne's Notting Hill home, found drugs, and arrested her. Anne Beverly died on September 6, 1996, after carefully putting her affairs in order and then consuming a large quantity of painkillers, tranquilizers, and alcohol. "Rumor has it that Sid Dust still circulates throughout terminal four."

xref.title: Final Illness and Legacy (2009-2010)
xref.body: In October 2009, Malcolm McLaren was diagnosed with mesothelioma, a form of lung cancer often linked to asbestos exposure. He died on April 8, 2010, at a hospital in Switzerland. His burial featured a coffin spray-painted with "Too Fast to Live, Too Young to Die," and Sid Vicious's version of "My Way" was played. His headstone encapsulates his philosophy with the epitaph: "Better a Spectacular Failure than a benign success."

xref.body: After Nancy Spungin's murder and Sid Vicious's arrest, Malcolm McLaren and Sid's mother immediately sought a high-profile lawyer for his defense. McLaren strongly believed Sid was innocent, theorizing that an unknown guest had robbed the couple and then stabbed Nancy, noting that $20,000 in royalty money was missing from their room. xref.title: Alleged Involvement in Spungen's Death
xref.body: According to a preferred theory, Rockets Red Glare, who supplied Sid and Nancy with drugs, allegedly arrived at the Chelsea Hotel between 3 and 5 AM on October 12, 1978, while Sid Vicious was unconscious. During this time, he is suspected of having stolen up to $20,000 and then murdered Nancy, whose death occurred between 5 and 9 AM. "At around 1.30 in the morning of October the 12th, Nancy called Rockets and asked him to bring some drugs. He arrived somewhere after 3 and stayed until about 5. Remember Sid is apparently completely unconscious at this point. The autopsy on Nancy suggested that she died between 5 and 9 am. The police report also says that a large amount of money was missing from the room, maybe as much as $20,000. Rockets was spotted at the hotel at around 4. There were two or three people who confirmed seeing him."

xref.body: While staying at the Chelsea Hotel, Sid Vicious and Nancy Spungen primarily consumed drugs, with heroin being their preferred substance, but also engaging with methadone, pot, and dilaudid. Sid Vicious experienced at least one overdose during the final weeks of Nancy's life. "Heroine was their favorite, but they also got into methadone, pots, delauded, and whatever else they could get their hands on."

xref.title: Early Performance with Sid Vicious
xref.body: On September 20, 1976, Sid Vicious played drums for a very early version of Siouxsie and the Banshees at the 100 Club Punk Special, where the group improvised interminably on the Lord's Prayer. "On September 20th, 1976, Sid somehow ended up playing drums for a very early version of Suzy in the Banshees at a two-day punk event called the 100 Club Punk Special."

xref.title: Early Punk Scene Figure and Guitar Teacher
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde was an American living in London at the heart of the burgeoning punk rock scene. She was a more skilled guitarist than many of her peers, even providing lessons to novices like Steve Jones and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols. Her rhythm guitar style was heavily influenced by James Brown's band. "She gave lessons to novices like Steve Jones and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fundraising Gig for New York Move
xref.body: Formed as a temporary group featuring Sid Vicious on vocals, Glenn Matlock (whom Sid had replaced in the Sex Pistols) on bass, Rats Scabies of The Damned on drums, and Steve New on guitar, this group played a quick solo gig at the Electric Ballroom in Camden on August 15, 1978. The purpose was to raise money for Sid and Nancy to fly to New York. "To raise money, there was a quick solo gig at the electric ballroom in Camden under the name Vicious White Kids."

xref.title: Girlfriend of Sid Vicious
xref.body: Nancy Spungen was the girlfriend of former Sex Pistol, Sid Vicious, and her death became one of the most infamous murders in music history. "Nancy was the girlfriend of ex-sexual Sidvicious."

xref.body: Anniversaries of the death of Ian Curtis of Joy Division were among the milestones discussed. "anniversaries of the deaths of people like Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols and Ian Curtis of Joy Division"

xref.title: Ill-Fated Only American Tour
xref.body: The Sex Pistols embarked on their one and only tour of America with manager Malcolm McLaren's "insane idea" to play out-of-the-way, "redneck" markets in the Deep South instead of major cities, leading to predictable chaos and hostility. "This is exactly what happened with Sid Vicious during the Sex Pistols, one and only two-er of America. Manager Malcolm McLaren had this insane idea. Instead of playing all the big markets across the US, the group would duck down into the deep south and play out of the way markets that were decidedly not punk-friendly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Sid Vicious's Bass Playing – Speed and Listening
xref.body: Sid Vicious claimed to have taught himself bass by staying up one night on speed, listening to a Ramones record. By morning, he could play along, an anecdote highlighting their raw, influential sound in the punk scene. "He stayed up one night on speed while listening to a Ramon's record. By morning, he could play along."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Sid Vicious's Early Busking
xref.body: Sid Vicious and John Lighten (Johnny Rotten) would busk by playing covers of Alice Cooper songs, with the "joke" being that they would play until they were paid to stop. "Sid and John Lighten picked up some spare change busking, usually by playing covers by Alice Cooper."

xref.title: Knife Ownership Inspiring Sid Vicious
xref.body: Steve Bator's of the Dead Boys owned a 007 hunting knife, which inspired Sid Vicious to purchase a similar one. This knife later became the weapon in Nancy Spungen's murder. "He wanted one because Steve Bader's of the Dead Boys had one."

xref.title: Knife Purchase with Sid Vicious
xref.body: Steve Lucky, a member of the Canadian band The Viletones, accompanied Sid Vicious when he purchased the 007 hunting knife on 42nd Street that would later be used in Nancy Spungen's murder. "Sid had bought it with a couple of friends, including Steve Lucky of the Canadian band The Vile Tones at a place on 42nd Street."

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Management Practices
xref.body: The financial arrangements orchestrated by the band's manager, Malcolm McLaren, were such that Sid Vicious did not receive much income from his time with the Sex Pistols. "And with the way things were arranged through the pistols manager, Malcolm McLaren, there really wasn't much of an income stream for Sid."

xref.title: Manager Malcolm McLaren's Recollection of Sid Vicious's Violence
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren recounted an incident from the American tour near San Antonio where Sid Vicious, heavily involved in drugs and eating knickerbocker glories, took offense to a family's rude comments about him at a restaurant. Sid then slashed the arm of the father with a pen knife, causing blood to spray onto his steak, terrifying onlookers. "He went round to the back of the gentleman that was eating his steak and chips and pulled his sleeve back and threw his arm over and above the man's head and over the man's plate up fairly high and withdrew a pen knife from his pocket and slashed his arm and all the blood blew out like ketchup over the man's steak."

xref.title: McLaren's Attempted Re-hiring of Matlock
xref.body: Two weeks after Matlock's departure, Malcolm McLaren called him, acknowledging that his replacement, Sid Vicious, was not working out and asked Matlock to rejoin the band. Matlock refused, stating it was "too late" and he wanted "none of you locked anymore." "What if Madlock had returned to the Sex Pistols? How would their future and their legend and myth and legacy turned out?"

xref.body: After the Sex Pistols, when Sid Vicious attempted a solo career in New York, a band was put together for him that featured "a few members of the New York dolls." "A band was put together featuring a few members of the New York dolls."

xref.title: Mick Jones's Involvement with Sid Vicious's Solo Band
xref.body: On "one or two occasions," Mick Jones of The Clash joined Sid Vicious's solo band during his attempt to launch a solo career in New York. "On one or two occasions, the group also featured Mick Jones of the clash."

xref.title: Nancy Spungen as Groupie – Followed the Drummer to England
xref.body: Nancy Spungen was a groupie of the Heartbreakers. She followed their drummer, Jerry Nolan, to England in an attempt to win him over, which eventually led to her encountering Sid Vicious. "When she followed Heartbreakers drummer Jerry Nolan to England to try and win him over, she stumbled onto this guy named Sid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nancy Spungen's Murder and Sid Vicious's Arrest
xref.body: Nancy Spungen died on October 12th, 1978, from a single knife wound to her abdomen after a party in their Chelsea Hotel room the previous night, October 11th. Sid Vicious had taken 22 tablets of a powerful sedative and passed out, only to wake up to find Nancy dead on the bathroom floor, covered in congealed blood. The autopsy determined she bled to death over at least three hours. The murder weapon was a 007 hunting knife Sid had purchased on 42nd Street, inspired by Steve Bator's of the Dead Boys. Sid was arrested and charged with second-degree murder, giving inconsistent statements about the event, ranging from not remembering to claiming he did it because he was "a dirty dog" or that she fell on the knife. "The cops were called and Sid was arrested and charged with her murder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Payment Strategy for Sid Vicious
xref.body: During the Sex Pistols' chaotic US tour, McLaren put Sid Vicious on a weekly stipend of $14, hoping that a lack of readily available cash might help him "keep him straight" from drug use. "McLaren had him on a weekly stipend of $14, thinking that maybe a lock of cash would keep him straight."

xref.title: Post-Sex Pistols Project
xref.body: Before his death, Sid Vicious was attempting to launch a career independent of the Sex Pistols with a new band called The Vicious White Kids. Some recordings from this project exist. xref.title: Punk Scene Roots
xref.body: Born William Broad, Billy Idol was deeply immersed in the original punk rock scene, actively following the Sex Pistols and associating with seminal figures like Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious before adopting his stage name and forming Generation X. "William Broad followed the pistols everywhere. He was deep into the original punk rock scene."

xref.title: Reaction to Sid Vicious's Violence
xref.body: After Sid Vicious assaulted journalist Nick Kent with a bicycle chain in June 1976, McLaren expressed dismay, calling Sid a "psychopath" and promising that he would never be allowed at their concerts again. "Malcolm McLaren though was mortified. He told Kent, oh God, that guy's a psychopath. He'll never be one of our concerts again. I promise that."

xref.title: Roadie Playing Sid's Bass Parts – Offstage
xref.body: Due to Sid Vicious's musical ineptitude and frequent inebriation, a roadie was often hired to play many of his bass parts offstage and unseen. This practice was noted during their tours, including the Dallas show where Sid's bass had broken strings. "Basically Sid was so inept as a musician, often so drunk and high that there's real doubt whether he ever played a note on stage with the pistols."

xref.title: Sid Vicious Audition
xref.body: Sid Vicious was considered for the lead vocalist position in The Damned but failed to show up for the audition. "Sid was considered for lead vocalist of the damned, but me forgot to show up for the audition."

xref.body: Sid Vicious was considered to be the lead singer of The Damned, a new punk band at the time. However, he failed to show up for the audition and did not get the gig. "It's also possible that he was considered to be the lead singer of another new punk band called The Damned."

xref.title: Sid Vicious Marriage Attempt
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde notably almost married Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols, an attempt to acquire the British equivalent of a green card to remain in the UK. This anecdote further illustrates her deep connections within the early punk scene. "And then there was also the time that she nearly married Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols just so she could stay in the UK."

xref.body: Chrissie Hynde almost entered into a marriage of convenience with Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols as a means to remain in the UK and continue her musical work. xref.title: Sid Vicious Stabbing Incident
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren recounted an incident during the ill-fated American tour where Sid Vicious, deeply involved in drugs, became agitated in a motel restaurant near San Antonio. While sitting near a family eating, Vicious, wearing a dirty black t-shirt with a swastika and his feet black from not taking off his boots for six months, heard rude comments about him. He then walked behind the gentleman, pulled back his sleeve, threw his arm over the man's head and plate, and slashed his arm with a pen knife, causing blood to spurt out "like ketchup" over the man's steak. This occurred in a place full of "red necky guys" and "long distance truck drivers," leading McLaren to fear for their lives. "He went round to the back of the gentleman that was eating his steak and chips and pulled his sleeve back and threw his arm over and above the man's head and over the man's plate up fairly high and withdrew a pen knife from his pocket and slashed his arm and all the blood blew out like ketchup over the man's steak."

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Background and Entry
xref.body: John Simon Richie, known as Sid Vicious, replaced Glenn Matlock as bass player. He was described as a violent, semi-literate hanger-on and had previously been a sometime drummer and saxophone player. Before joining the group, he worked as a shop assistant in a sex shop. He considered Johnny Rotten an "old enemy" from the start, but after seeing the band perform, he thought they were "really wonderful" and admired their honesty, citing the Bill Grundy incident as genuine. "His replacement was a violent semi-literate hangar on and sometime drummer and saxophone player named John Simon Richie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Death and Ashes Disposition
xref.body: Sid Vicious died of a heroin overdose in his sleep in the early morning hours of February 2nd, 1979, at 63 Bank Street in Greenwich Village, New York, while out on bail awaiting trial for the death of Nancy Spungen. He was cremated because no funeral home would take his business. A legend, though unproven, suggests he died with a note asking to be buried next to Nancy in his leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. Another popular, but false, myth claims his mother, Beverly, spilled his ashes at Heathrow Airport. Semi-reliable sources claim his ashes never left America, with his mother reportedly taking them to King David Cemetery in Philadelphia, where Nancy was buried, hopping a fence to dump them on Nancy's grave against her parents' wishes. "Sid Vicious, ex of the sex pistols, died of a heroin overdose in his sleep in the early morning hours of February 2nd, 1979."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Fight with Bodyguard
xref.body: During the American tour, Sid Vicious challenged his bodyguard, Glenn Allison—a 6'5", 250-pound Vietnam veteran—to a fight. Allison responded by grabbing Sid by the throat, smacking his head against the ceiling, and then repeatedly against a sink. After the beating, Sid, through bloody teeth, declared, "You're good enough. I like you. Now we can be friends." "Sid challenged him to a fight. Allison began by grabbing Sid by the throat and smacked his head up against the ceiling. And when Allison finished pummeling Sid's head against a sink half a dozen times, Sid said through bloody teeth, you're good enough. I like you. Now we can be friends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Inability to Play Bass
xref.body: Glenn Matlock was fired from the Sex Pistols in 1977 for allegedly liking The Beatles, which was considered a "crime" within the band. His replacement was a fan named Sid Vicious, who was chosen for his cool look and punk-rock attitude, even though he could not play the bass. During the band's last tour in America in late 1977 and their final original show at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978, Sid appeared on stage but did not play a note; roadies were instructed to unplug him, and another musician played his bass parts behind the amplifiers.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Membership – Early Band
xref.body: Sid Vicious was part of a group called Flowers of Romance, one of his early musical projects before he joined the Sex Pistols. "And he was also part of a group called Flowers of Romance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's On-Tour Conduct
xref.body: During the American tour, Sid Vicious was notoriously problematic, spitting at people and instigating fights with anyone who looked at him in a way he perceived as offensive. He famously used his bass guitar to swing "like a cricket bat at people's heads." His behavior was so extreme that he was even beaten up by his own bodyguard a few days into the tour. Due to his drug use, he was considered "too stupider to stone to actually play," so his amplifier was never actually hooked up, with a roadie offstage playing all his bass parts. "Sid Vicious wasn't much help. He spit at everybody and he picked fights with anyone who looked at him funny."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Pogo Invention
xref.body: Sid Vicious, who later became the bassist for the Sex Pistols, is credited in legend as the inventor of the Pogo dance. He reportedly started pogoing to mock non-punks who attended the band's shows, as he felt they didn't truly belong. Another account from Shane McGowan suggests Sid's tight leather poncho restricted his dance movements to just jumping. "legend says he started Pogoing as a way of mocking non-punks who came to see the pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Pogo Origin Story
xref.body: Shane McGowan, the singer of The Pogs and a big punk fan, offered an alternative explanation for Sid Vicious's Pogo dance. He suggested that Sid's dance style was a result of him wearing a tight leather poncho that restricted his movements, forcing him to simply jump up and down. "He says Sid's dance was the result of him insisting on wearing a tight leather poncho that restricted his dance movements to just jumping up and down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Subsequent Jailing and Death
xref.body: After being bailed out following Nancy Spungen's murder charge, Sid Vicious was re-jailed for 55 days for slashing a man's face with a broken beer bottle. He was bailed out again before the murder case could proceed to trial, but he died of an overdose. "He stayed there for 55 days before he was bailed out again. But before the case could come to trial, Sid died of an overdose."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Tenure
xref.body: Sid Vicious was briefly a member of Flowers of Romance, but the band "didn't amount to anything." "Eventually, he found his way into a band called Flowers of Romance, but that didn't amount to anything."

xref.title: Siouxsie Sioux's Early Band
xref.body: Formed by Susan Ballion (who became Siouxsie Sioux) after being inspired by the Sex Pistols, this punk band featured future Sex Pistols member Sid Vicious on drums. "forming a band called Flowers of Romance, which featured future sex pistols, Sid Vicious on drums."

xref.title: Steve Lucky's Commentary on Sid Vicious – Foreshadowed Death
xref.body: Steve Lucky, a member of the Canadian band The Vialtoons, was present when Sid Vicious purchased the knife later implicated in Nancy Spungen's death. He commented that Sid's death was unsurprising and "bathed in banality," as Sid "really did give off the vibe that he really clearly was not fully here." "Sid was bathed in benality. You know, and you could see it coming a mile away."

xref.title: Subversive US Tour Strategy
xref.body: Instead of hitting major markets, manager Malcolm McLaren designed a "subversive" strategy for the US tour, planning a major swing into the punk-unfriendly Southern US. This tour, however, "did not go well," with hostile crowds and Sid Vicious often being too strung out to perform effectively. "But instead of hitting all the major markets, McLaren thought it would be very subversive, very punk, if the pistols made a big swing into the punk, unfriendly, southern US."

xref.title: Suspected in Nancy Spungen Murder
xref.body: Rockets Red Glare, whose real name was Michael Mora, was a New York actor and drug dealer considered the favorite suspect by many in the unsolved murder of Nancy Spungen, girlfriend of Sid Vicious. "The favorite suspect by most is a New York actor and drug dealer who went by the name Rockets Red Glare. His real name was Michael Mora, by the way."

xref.title: US Tour Visa Troubles
xref.body: The band faced significant difficulties obtaining working visas for their planned late 1977 American tour due to the criminal records of its members. Johnny Rotten had a minor drug charge, Steve Jones and Paul Cook had past theft charges, and Sid Vicious had a record including drug charges, assault on a police officer, attempted grand theft auto, criminal damage, and possession of a dangerous weapon. "Getting working visas for these yobbs proved to be very difficult."

xref.title: Unsolved Mystery - Suspects and Theories
xref.body: While Sid Vicious was charged with her murder, many dispute his guilt, suggesting a New York actor and drug dealer named Rockets Red Glare (Michael Mora) as a primary alternative suspect. A theory posits that Rockets brought drugs to the hotel around 1:30 AM on October 12, stayed until 5 AM while Sid was unconscious, stole a large amount of money (up to $20,000), and then murdered Nancy, whose autopsy indicated she died between 5 and 9 AM. "The favorite suspect by most is a New York actor and drug dealer who went by the name Rockets Red Glare. He was a hangar on with Sid and Nancy, often supplying them with drugs. At around 1.30 in the morning of October the 12th, Nancy called Rockets and asked him to bring some drugs. He arrived somewhere after 3 and stayed until about 5. Remember Sid is apparently completely unconscious at this point. The autopsy on Nancy suggested that she died between 5 and 9 am. The police report also says that a large amount of money was missing from the room, maybe as much as $20,000. Rockets was spotted at the hotel at around 4. There were two or three people who confirmed seeing him."
